Apple___Apple_scab.description: A serious fungal disease affecting Malus species causing olive-green to black velvety spots on leaves and fruit, causing premature defoliation and unmarketable fruit.
symptoms: Olive-green to velvety brown-black lesions on upper leaf surfaces
Distorted, curled, or dwarfed leaves
Premature leaf drop in severe mid-summer infections
Scabby, corky, dark brown lesions on the fruit surface
treatment: Apply preventive fungicides such as captan, mancozeb, or myclobutanil at green tip stage
Use sulfur-based or copper sprays for certified organic orchards
Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn to eliminate overwintering fungal ascospores
Prune the canopy during dormancy to promote rapid leaf drying
prevention: Plant scab-resistant cultivars such as Enterprise, Liberty, Prima, and GoldRush
Ensure wide tree spacing for maximum sunlight penetration and air circulation
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that keeps leaves wet for over 9 hours

Apple___Black_rot.description: Black rot attacks fruit, leaves, and bark, causing distinctive frogeye leaf spots, branch cankers, and a firm, dark mummified fruit rot.
symptoms: Small purple leaf spots that enlarge into circular lesions with light brown centers and dark purple margins (frogeye)
Firm brown fruit rot with concentric rings, later turning coal-black and leathery
Sunken reddish-brown cankers on twigs and main limbs
treatment: Prune out dead wood, fire-blighted shoots, and limb cankers at least 15 cm below visible lesions
Apply thiophanate-methyl, captan, or copper-based sprays from petal fall through cover sprays
Remove and bury or burn all mummified apples hanging on branches or on the orchard floor
prevention: Maintain tree vigor through balanced fertilization and drought mitigation
Sterilize pruning shears between cuts using 70% isopropyl alcohol
Prevent insect and mechanical wounding of developing apples

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: A heteroecious rust requiring two alternate hosts (apples and Eastern red cedars / junipers) to complete its complex multi-stage life cycle.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange circular spots on the upper leaf surface in late spring
Raised orange pustules developing tiny black dots (pycnia) at spot centers
Tube-like projection structures (aecia) on leaf undersides shedding powdery spores
Premature defoliation and fruit distortion in severe seasons
treatment: Apply targeted fungicides (myclobutanil, mancozeb, or triadimefon) between pink bud stage and petal fall
Remove galls from nearby juniper and cedar trees before gelatinous orange telial horns emerge in spring
prevention: Eliminate Eastern red cedar trees within a 1 to 2 mile radius of the orchard where possible
Plant rust-immune or resistant varieties such as Honeycrisp, Liberty, William's Pride, or Redfree
Monitor spring rainfall events occurring concurrently with temperatures between 10-24°C

Apple___healthy.description: Leaves show vibrant uniform green pigmentation, intact margins, balanced venation, and absence of fungal, bacterial, or necrotic lesions.
symptoms: Glossy, uniform deep-green leaf blades
No chlorotic halos, necrotic spots, or fungal powder
Normal leaf expansion and vigor
treatment: No curative treatment required
Maintain standard seasonal nutritional schedule
prevention: Routine integrated pest management (IPM) monitoring
Apply balanced foliar micronutrients (Zinc, Boron, Calcium) during early fruit set
Ensure consistent soil moisture management

Blueberry___healthy.description: Blueberry foliage exhibits optimal vegetative health, correct acidic-soil nutrient uptake, and absence of rust or fungal leaf spots.
symptoms: Clean, dark green, oval-shaped leaves with healthy waxy cuticle
Absence of red rings, anthracnose spots, or tip dieback
treatment: No treatment required
prevention: Maintain soil pH between 4.5 and 5.2 using elemental sulfur or organic pine needle mulch
Use drip irrigation to keep root zone consistently moist without wetting the canopy
Ensure good soil drainage to prevent Phytophthora root rot

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew attacks succulent young leaves, green shoots, and fruit stems of both sweet and sour cherry trees.
symptoms: White to grayish powdery fungal patches on young foliage and shoots
Upward curling, crinkling, and distortion of newly emerging leaves
Stunted terminal shoot growth with shortened internodes
Fruit may become blemished, distorted, or fail to mature
treatment: Apply potassium bicarbonate, horticultural oils, or sulfur formulations early in the season
Use systemic fungicides (quinoxyfen, triflumizole, or myclobutanil) upon first sign of mildew colonies
prevention: Prune trees annually to enhance air flow and sun exposure inside the inner canopy
Avoid high-rate late-season nitrogen applications that stimulate susceptible tender flush growth

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.description: Vigorous cherry foliage displaying characteristic serrated green leaves free from shot-hole, powdery mildew, or leaf curl.
symptoms: Intact serrated leaf margins without perforations or yellow halos
Lush green coloring across new and mature terminal branches
treatment: No treatment needed
prevention: Regular protective copper spray at leaf fall to guard against bacterial canker
Maintain good orchard hygiene and annual canopy pruning

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: One of the most destructive foliar diseases of maize worldwide, favored by warm, humid weather and minimum-tillage continuous corn systems.
symptoms: Small, tan-colored spots with yellow halos that expand into long, narrow, rectangular lesions
Lesions strictly delimited by parallel leaf veins (blocky rectangular shape)
Lesions turn grayish-brown when fungal spores sporulate on leaf surfaces
Extensive leaf blighting and premature crop senescence
treatment: Apply strobilurin (azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin) or triazole (propiconazole) fungicides at VT-R1 growth stages
Ensure economic threshold is evaluated before late reproductive spraying
prevention: Select corn hybrids with high polygenic resistance ratings against Cercospora
Rotate fields out of corn for at least 1-2 years to non-host crops like soybeans
Manage crop residue through tillage if disease pressure has been historically severe

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Airborne fungal rust that infects sweet corn and field maize, flourishing in cool to moderate temperatures with high relative humidity.
symptoms: Golden-brown to cinnamon-brown elongated pustules scattered across both leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture the epidermis to release powdery reddish-brown urediniospores
Chlorotic halos surrounding older pustules, turning brownish-black near maturity
Severe infection causes leaf chlorosis and reduced photosynthetic capacity
treatment: Apply triazole or strobilurin fungicides early if pustules appear prior to tasseling and weather is cool and wet
Monitor sweet corn closely as it is generally more vulnerable than field corn
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant maize hybrids possessing the Rp gene
Plant early in the season to evade peak spore migration from southern regions

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: A devastating fungal disease producing large cigar-shaped necrotic lesions that can cause significant grain yield loss when established before silking.
symptoms: Long, elliptical, grayish-green or tan lesions measuring 2.5 to 15 cm in length
Distinct cigar-shaped lesions with smooth rounded ends (not restricted by leaf veins)
Dark olive fungal sporulation inside lesions under damp morning conditions
Complete premature drying of entire corn leaves mimicking drought stress
treatment: Foliar fungicide application (strobilurin/triazole combinations) between V14 and early silking
Target spraying if lower leaves show lesions and extended dew periods are forecasted
prevention: Plant corn hybrids featuring resistance genes (such as Ht1, Ht2, Ht3, or HtN)
Implement a minimum 2-year crop rotation with non-cereal crops
Deep plow infected crop residue to accelerate biological decomposition of fungal mycelium

Corn_(maize)___healthy.description: Healthy maize foliage displays vibrant dark green arching leaves with prominent midribs, optimal nitrogen content, and total absence of foliar blights.
symptoms: Broad, deep-green, upright leaves with robust turgor
Smooth leaf blades with intact parallel venation and no pustules or chlorosis
treatment: No treatment required
prevention: Maintain balanced soil N-P-K nutrition and split-apply nitrogen during rapid vegetative growth
Scout fields systematically at V6, V10, and VT stages

Grape___Black_rot.description: A severe fungal blight of cultivated grapevines in warm, humid climates, destroying both foliage and developing berry clusters.
symptoms: Circular reddish-brown spots on leaves with small black dots (pycnidia) arranged in rings near margins
Berries develop light brown sunken spots that rapidly enlarge
Infected berries shrivel into hard, wrinkled, jet-black mummies within days
treatment: Apply myclobutanil, tebuconazole, or azoxystrobin fungicides from early bloom until 4 weeks post-bloom
Remove and destroy all mummified grape clusters and infected canes during winter pruning
prevention: Canopy management: shoot thinning and leaf pulling to maximize air movement through clusters
Maintain weed-free ground beneath grape trellises to reduce ground-level humidity

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: A complex wood-decay disease of grapevines affecting vascular tissues, causing characteristic tiger-striped foliage, berry speckling, and eventual vine apoplexy.
symptoms: Interveinal chlorosis and necrosis creating a distinctive 'tiger-stripe' pattern on mature leaves
Small, dark purple-brown spots on fruit berries resembling measles spots
Sudden wilting and collapse of entire vine canopies in hot summer weather (apoplexy)
Spongy brown or white wood rot visible in cross-sections of the trunk
treatment: No curative chemical treatment exists once internal wood is colonized
Cut back infected cordons or trunks to healthy wood and retrain a new sucker trunk
Apply wound sealant or Trichoderma biocontrol immediately to large pruning cuts
prevention: Prune vines late in the dormant season when pruning wounds heal much more rapidly
Disinfect pruning tools between vines, especially when operating in mature vineyards
Source certified disease-free grafted planting stocks

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: Late-season foliar disease causing angular leaf lesions that can induce premature defoliation, weakening vine reserves for subsequent seasons.
symptoms: Irregular, angular, dark brown to black spots visible on upper leaf surfaces
Under high humidity, a velvety olive-brown fungal layer appears on lesion undersides
Leaves turn yellow, dry out, and drop prematurely from the vine
treatment: Apply copper hydroxide or mancozeb sprays after mid-summer if symptoms spread
Ensure post-harvest sprays if defoliation threatens cane hardening before frost
prevention: Improve canopy ventilation by removing excessive lateral shoots and selective shoot positioning
Collect and compost or bury fallen autumn leaves to eliminate overwintering inoculum

Grape___healthy.description: Grapevine foliage displays expansive palmately lobed leaves with deep green chlorophyll saturation, clear veins, and productive tendrils.
symptoms: Uniform bright to dark green lobed leaf blades with crisp margins
No chlorotic mottling, leaf scorching, or downy mildew patches
treatment: No treatment required
prevention: Standard preventative viticultural canopy management and balanced drip fertigation
Monitor for leafhoppers, phylloxera, and early fungal symptoms

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).pathogen: Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus (Bacterium, transmitted by Asian Citrus Psyllid)
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: The most destructive citrus disease globally. The phloem-limited bacterium blocks nutrient flow, starving the tree and ruining fruit quality.
symptoms: Blotchy, asymmetrical yellow mottling across leaf veins (one side of leaf differs from other)
Yellow veins and corky vein swelling on mature leaves
Small, lopsided, bitter fruit that stays green at the blossom end (greening)
Extensive branch dieback, premature fruit drop, and tree mortality within 3-5 years
treatment: There is currently no cure for infected trees; remove and destroy confirmed infected trees
Aggressively control the vector, Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri), using systemic insecticides (imidacloprid) and biological controls (Tamarixia radiata)
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free nursery stock cultivated in insect-proof screenhouses
Implement area-wide psyllid eradication and scout using yellow sticky traps
Optimize foliar nutritional therapy (Zinc, Manganese, Boron) to support tree resilience

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial pathogen causing defoliation, twig dieback, and pitted unmarketable fruit in peaches, nectarines, and plums.
symptoms: Water-soaked angular spots on leaves, becoming purple-black and dropping out (shot-hole effect)
Severe leaf yellowing starting near the leaf tip and early summer defoliation
Deep, pitted, cracked lesions on the peach fruit with gummy exudates
Small cankers on young spring twigs
treatment: Apply fixed copper bactericides at bud break and early dormancy
Apply oxytetracycline bactericide during bloom and shuck split periods in high-risk seasons
Avoid high-pressure overhead spraying which spreads bacterial inoculum
prevention: Select resistant cultivars such as Biscoe, Candor, Clayton, or Contender
Plant windbreaks around orchards to reduce sandblasting and wind injury which allow bacterial entry
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization that stimulates succulent susceptible growth

Peach___healthy.description: Lush, lanceolate peach leaves displaying smooth, rich green color and robust internode extension without leaf curl or spots.
symptoms: Smooth, vibrant, lance-shaped leaves with fine serrations
No puckering, reddish thickening (peach leaf curl), or shot-holes
treatment: No treatment required
prevention: Apply single dormant copper spray at 50% leaf drop in autumn to prevent leaf curl fungus
Prune to open center (vase shape) for optimal sunlight distribution

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Devastating disease of bell peppers in warm, rainy weather, resulting in heavy defoliation and sunscald of exposed developing peppers.
symptoms: Small, circular, water-soaked spots on leaf undersides that turn dark brown with greasy margins
Spots enlarge and coalesce, causing widespread chlorosis and dramatic leaf drop
Rough, raised, warty brown lesions on green and ripening pepper pods
treatment: Apply copper hydroxide combined with mancozeb to overcome copper-tolerant bacterial strains
Utilize bacteriophage foliar sprays or acibenzolar-S-methyl for systemic acquired resistance induction
prevention: Use certified pathogen-free seeds treated with hot water (50°C for 25 min) or bleach
Plant resistant commercial varieties featuring race-specific resistance genes (Bs1, Bs2, Bs3)
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers to prevent water splash dissemination

Pepper,_bell___healthy.description: Healthy pepper plant foliage features glossy, deep green, pointed leaves with intact cuticles and sturdy upright stem branching.
symptoms: Uniform dark green, glossy leaves with smooth margins
Absence of curling, mosaic mottling, or necrotic spots
treatment: No treatment required
prevention: Mulch soil with reflective or organic straw mulch to moderate soil temperature and suppress weeds
Maintain steady soil calcium levels to prevent blossom-end rot on fruits

Potato___Early_blight.description: Ubiquitous fungal disease occurring annually on older potato foliage, characterized by target-like concentric ring lesions.
symptoms: Brown to black circular or angular spots on older lower leaves first
Distinct concentric rings within lesions resembling a target board or bullseye
Yellow chlorotic halos surrounding expanding lesions
Tuber infection creates dry, dark, sunken, leathery surface lesions
treatment: Apply protectant fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb) when early signs appear on lower leaves
Alternate with strobilurins (azoxystrobin) or SDHI fungicides (boscalid) to prevent fungal resistance
prevention: Practice a 3-year crop rotation out of solanaceous crops (tomatoes, eggplants, peppers)
Ensure adequate nitrogen and potassium fertility; plant stress dramatically increases susceptibility
Avoid late afternoon sprinkler irrigation that extends overnight leaf wetness

Potato___Late_blight.description: The historical cause of the Irish Potato Famine; an extremely aggressive, fast-moving water mold capable of destroying entire fields within a week under cool, wet conditions.
symptoms: Pale green, water-soaked lesions that rapidly turn dark brown to purplish-black
Delicate white fuzzy sporulation visible on the underside of leaves at the margins of lesions under damp conditions
Foul-smelling, decaying foliage that collapses completely
Tubers develop a dry, corky, reddish-brown rot spreading inwards from the skin
treatment: Apply systemic oomycete-specific fungicides (metalaxyl-M, cymoxanil, dimethomorph, or fluopicolide) immediately upon regional disease alert
Destroy infected cull piles and harvest tops before harvesting tubers in wet conditions
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free seed tubers
Eliminate volunteer potato plants and cull piles from previous harvests
Monitor disease forecasting platforms (e.g., BlightCast) and spray preventatively ahead of rain

Potato___healthy.description: Robust compound potato leaves with lush green foliage, sturdy petioles, and active tuberization support.
symptoms: Full, healthy compound green leaves without curling or spots
Uniform vigorous canopy growth without wilting or premature yellowing
treatment: No treatment required
prevention: Hill up soil around stems properly to protect expanding tubers from greening and fungal spores
Implement preventive IPM scouting weekly throughout tuber development

Raspberry___healthy.description: Healthy compound serrate leaves displaying bright green color, white woolly undersides, and vigorous cane shoots.
symptoms: Clean 3 to 5-foliate leaves with silvery-white lower surfaces
Absence of spur blight lesions, yellow rust pustules, or cane anthracnose
treatment: No treatment required
prevention: Thin floricanes after summer harvest to stimulate strong new primocanes
Install trellis support systems to keep canes off the ground and improve air flow

Soybean___healthy.description: Trifoliate soybean foliage with rich green color, optimal nodulation-driven nitrogen status, and clear leaf surfaces.
symptoms: Uniform trifoliate leaves with vibrant green coloration and smooth leaf blades
Absence of frogeye spots, downy mildew, or sudden death syndrome interveinal chlorosis
treatment: No treatment required
prevention: Inoculate seeds with Bradyrhizobium japonicum before planting for biological nitrogen fixation
Maintain standard crop rotation cycles with non-legume crops (corn, wheat)

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: A very common foliar fungal disease of cucurbits that covers leaves in white talcum-powder-like patches, reducing fruit yield and quality.
symptoms: White to dusty gray fungal growth appearing initially as round spots on crowns and lower leaf surfaces
White powder spreads rapidly to cover entire leaf blades, petioles, and stems
Leaves turn yellow, dry out, become brittle, and die prematurely
Sunscald on developing squash fruit due to loss of protective canopy cover
treatment: Spray potassium bicarbonate, neem oil, or dilute milk spray (1:9 ratio) at first sign of powder
Use chemical fungicides (triflumizole, quinoxyfen, or myclobutanil) rotating chemical classes to avoid resistance
prevention: Plant powdery mildew-resistant squash varieties (e.g. Success PM, Dunja)
Ensure wide spacing between plants and rows to facilitate air drying and ventilation
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which produces overly lush, highly susceptible foliage

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: A prevalent fungal disease producing countless small purple blotches on strawberry leaves, reducing crown vigor and berry yields.
symptoms: Small, irregular, dark purple to reddish-purple spots on upper leaf surfaces
Spots enlarge and coalesce without clear white centers (unlike leaf spot)
Entire leaf turns reddish, then brown and parched, giving the plant a scorched appearance
Fruit stems (pedicels) can be girdled, causing small, sour, unmarketable berries
treatment: Apply protectant fungicides (captan, pyraclostrobin, or copper) before bloom and post-harvest renovation
Remove and destroy heavily diseased foliage during post-harvest bed renovation
prevention: Plant certified disease-free strawberry runner plants
Utilize drip irrigation and avoid overhead sprinkling that keeps leaves wet overnight
Thin out dense strawberry beds to lower canopy humidity

Strawberry___healthy.description: Vigorous strawberry crowns with healthy dark green trifoliate leaves, strong petioles, and productive runner stolons.
symptoms: Glossy, deep-green trifoliate leaves with cleanly serrated margins
No purple spots, white mold, angular water-soaked lesions, or powdery mildew
treatment: No treatment required
prevention: Apply clean straw or plastic mulch beneath berries to prevent soil splash onto foliage
Renovate beds annually after harvest and maintain balanced slow-release nutrition

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: A major bacterial disease of field tomatoes in humid and warm climates, leading to severe leaf drop, blossom blight, and unmarketable spotted fruit.
symptoms: Small, greasy, water-soaked circular to angular dark brown spots on leaves
Spots often develop a thin yellow chlorotic halo
Severe blighting of foliage causing leaf death and severe sunscald on exposed green fruit
Raised, rough, scab-like spots with sunken centers on green and ripening tomatoes
treatment: Apply copper hydroxide bactericide tank-mixed with mancozeb for synergistic activity
Apply bacteriophage biological controls (e.g. AgriPhage) targeting Xanthomonas strains
Do not work in fields when tomato foliage is wet
prevention: Disinfect seed using hot water treatment (50°C for 25 minutes) before sowing
Practice a minimum 2 to 3-year crop rotation out of tomatoes, peppers, and eggplants
Utilize drip irrigation to keep canopy completely dry

Tomato___Early_blight.description: One of the most widespread fungal diseases of tomatoes, affecting leaves, stems, and fruit, typically starting on older foliage near the ground.
symptoms: Circular brown spots with distinct concentric rings (target board pattern) on lower leaves first
Yellowing of leaf tissue surrounding the concentric target lesions
Lower leaves turn completely brown, dry up, and drop from the vine
Dark, leathery, sunken spots near the stem end of developing tomato fruits
treatment: Apply bio-fungicides (Bacillus subtilis, copper) or chemical protectants (chlorothalonil, mancozeb)
Rotate with systemic fungicides (difenoconazole, azoxystrobin) for severe infestations
Prune off bottom 12 inches of lower foliage once plants are established to prevent soil splash
prevention: Apply heavy organic or black plastic mulch under tomato plants to block soil-to-leaf spore splashing
Stake, trellis, or cage tomato plants to ensure upright growth and optimal air circulation
Clean up and destroy all tomato crop debris at the end of the growing season

Tomato___Late_blight.description: An aggressive, destructive pathogen capable of decimating an entire tomato patch within a week during cool, wet, foggy weather.
symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked greenish-black lesions on leaves that rapidly turn papery brown
Delicate white cottony fungal growth on the undersides of lesions in high humidity
Dark brown to black greasy lesions on petioles and main stems
Firm, greasy, rough brown lesions on green and ripening tomato fruits that rot rapidly
treatment: Apply targeted oomycete fungicides (mandipropamid, cyazofamid, fluopicolide, or chlorothalonil) immediately upon local blight alerts
Immediately remove and bag heavily infected plants to stop spore clouds from infecting neighboring farms
prevention: Plant late-blight resistant tomato varieties such as Defiant Ph-R, Mountain Magic, or Iron Lady
Avoid overhead watering and provide maximum spacing between tomato rows
Destroy any volunteer tomato and potato plants emerging near the garden

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: A primarily greenhouse and high-tunnel disease of tomatoes that thrives in high relative humidity (above 85%) and stagnant air.
symptoms: Pale green or yellowish spots with indefinite margins on the upper leaf surface
Dense, velvety, olive-green to brown fungal mold growth directly beneath the spots on leaf undersides
Leaves curl, turn completely yellow, wither, and drop, starting from the base of the plant upward
treatment: Apply copper-based fungicides or biofungicides (Bacillus amyloliquefaciens) at first sign of mold
Apply chlorothalonil or cyazofamid for severe greenhouse infections
prevention: Increase greenhouse ventilation and use horizontal circulation fans to maintain humidity below 80%
Space plants generously and prune suckers to open the canopy to air movement
Plant resistant greenhouse cultivars containing Cf resistance genes

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: A highly destructive foliar fungal disease that causes severe progressive defoliation from the base upward, exposing fruit to sunscald.
symptoms: Numerous small, circular spots (1.5 to 3 mm) with dark brown margins and sunken grayish-white centers
Tiny, black specks (pycnidia fruiting bodies) visible in the center of mature spots with a hand lens
Heavily infected leaves turn yellow, curl up, wither, and drop prematurely
Defoliation progresses rapidly up the vine after fruit set
treatment: Apply copper fungicides or chlorothalonil every 7 to 10 days during warm, rainy weather
Strip off infected lower leaves as soon as first spots appear to slow upward spread
prevention: Practice 3-year crop rotation without solanaceous crops
Mulch plants with straw or plastic to eliminate soil rain-splash onto lower leaves
Always stake or trellis vines and water only at the soil line with drip hoses

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Microscopic sap-feeding arachnids that proliferate in hot, dry, dusty conditions, sucking chlorophyll and moisture from tomato leaf cells.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling (tiny dots) peppered across the upper leaf surfaces
Leaves take on a bronzed, dusty, chlorotic, or bleached appearance
Fine silky webbing visible on leaf undersides and between stems
Severe infestation causes complete leaf drying, leaf drop, and plant stunting
treatment: Spray insecticidal soap, horticultural oil, or neem oil directly onto leaf undersides
Release beneficial predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus californicus)
Use targeted miticides (abamectin, bifenazate, or spiromesifen) if organic measures are insufficient
prevention: Keep garden pathways and adjacent borders watered to suppress dry dust clouds that favor mites
Avoid broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids that eliminate natural predatory insects and cause mite flare-ups
Overhead misting can temporarily discourage mite population buildup in dry periods

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Fungal pathogen of warm, humid tropical and subtropical regions that infects leaves, stems, and fruit.
symptoms: Small, pinpoint brown spots that expand into circular brown lesions with light brown centers
Lesions exhibit concentric rings resembling a target (similar to early blight but spots are smaller and more numerous)
Extensive blighting and yellowing of the surrounding foliar tissue
Sunken brown lesions on the fruit with dark margins
treatment: Apply azoxystrobin, chlorothalonil, or copper fungicides at the first sign of symptoms
Alternate fungicide chemical classes to prevent fungal resistance
prevention: Maintain adequate row spacing to encourage rapid drying of foliage after rain or dew
Avoid planting near older cucurbit or solanaceous plantings that may host the pathogen
Incorporate or destroy crop debris immediately following final harvest

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.pathogen: Begomovirus (Virus, transmitted by Sweetpotato Whitefly Bemisia tabaci)
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: A devastating viral disease spread by whiteflies. Infected young plants are severely stunted and produce virtually no harvestable fruit.
symptoms: Severe upward cupping, curling, and crumpling of leaf margins
Marked interveinal chlorosis with leaves becoming pale yellow, especially on new growth
Noticeably reduced leaf size (shoestring appearance)
Severe plant stunting, bushy erect habit, and abortion of flowers before fruit set
treatment: There is no chemical cure for plant viruses; promptly pull out and bag infected plants to prevent vector transmission
Control whitefly vectors using insecticidal soaps, neem oil, yellow sticky traps, or systemic insecticides (imidacloprid, spirotetramat)
prevention: Plant TYLCV-resistant or tolerant hybrid varieties (such as Tygress, Charger, or Red Bounty)
Install fine insect-proof mesh netting (50-mesh) on greenhouse and nursery vents
Use UV-reflective silver plastic mulches which repel whitefly vectors from landing

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: An exceptionally stable and persistent plant virus easily transmitted by physical contact, contaminated tools, pruning shears, and workers hands.
symptoms: Mottled light and dark green mosaic patterns across leaves
Distortion, puckering, curling, and fern-like narrowing (shoestring) of leaflets
Stunting of plant growth and yellowish-bronze discoloration
Internal brown browning and blotchy ripening of tomato fruit
treatment: No cure exists for viral infection; immediately rogue and destroy infected plants
Wash hands and disinfect all tools in non-fat dry milk solution (20%) or 10% trisodium phosphate (TSP) after handling plants
prevention: Plant certified ToMV-resistant cultivars (designated by 'T' or 'ToMV' on seed packets)
Tobacco users must thoroughly scrub hands with soap before touching tomato seedlings, as tobacco carries related tobamoviruses
Do not save seeds from infected plants

Tomato___healthy.description: Vibrant compound leaves with deep green coloration, robust glandular trichomes, strong stems, and vigorous flowering trusses.
symptoms: Lush, deep green compound leaves with characteristic aroma and firm texture
No chlorotic mottling, necrosis, curling, wilting, or fungal sporulation
treatment: No treatment required
prevention: Prune lower suckers to maintain balance between vegetative growth and fruit production
Provide consistent watering with drip lines to prevent blossom-end rot and fruit splitting
Apply balanced N-P-K fertilizer with added calcium and magnesium throughout fruiting
